attribution.note: Zitron's own words on his newsletter, in his own voice.

semantics.note: The firm 'absolutely has to' wording supports reading this as a conditional. The antecedent (over $2T annual AI revenue by 2030) and both consequences are kept. 'Makes sense' is partly evaluative.

contract.note: Reading 'none' and 'neither' literally, and counting financing as part of ability to pay, is fair and ordinary. Having no return threshold for 'makes sense' is flagged. None of this matters before 2030.

evidence.note: Anthropic S-1 risk factor dated 2026-10-26, before the cutoff. It only says compute forecasts are uncertain. It says nothing about the revenue antecedent, payment outcomes or whether the capex makes sense.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast with a 2030 horizon, and the evaluation date is 2026-10-28. Whether the revenue antecedent holds is unknown, and there has been no conclusive early event. The only evidence item is a risk disclosure that settles nothing, so the claim is not scored yet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The categorical present-tense claim is kept. The Jane Street exception in the next sentence is handled by the contract.

contract.note: The result depends on whether xAI counts as a 'hyperscaler'. The contract reads hyperscaler as a large cloud provider, and an AI lab buying compute for its own models is not one. That is a fair, ordinary reading. Using Q1 2026 for 'at present' is reasonable, since these deals were ongoing.

evidence.note: Apollo announcement of 2026-01-07, as a party to the deal: a $5.4B compute lease to an xAI subsidiary to train Grok. This is a multibillion-dollar compute buyer outside the named groups.
Mississippi governor's release of 2026-01-08: xAI is investing over $20B in its own data center, with operations due February 2026. This confirms large-scale own-use compute buying.
Jane Street's $6B CoreWeave deal, April 2026. Zitron names Jane Street as the exception, though his 'few hundred million' understates it. Not decisive.

reviews.rationale: Disclosures from parties to the deals show xAI leasing and building compute at multibillion-dollar scale in Q1 2026 to develop its own models. xAI is an AI developer, not a cloud hyperscaler under an ordinary reading, so the claim that no other major purchasers exist is contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own calculation. He cites Huang's and Sightline's figures only as inputs.

semantics.note: The 'at face value' antecedent is kept. But the claim is an arithmetic implication that can be checked at publication, not a forecast of future costs, so it is better classed as an observation, as the contract treats it.

contract.note: Zitron supplied both inputs himself (190GW and $80–100B per GW). Multiplying them is exactly what his sentence asserts.

evidence.note: Sightline's February 2026 outlook confirms the 190GW input (announced capacity since 2024).
Transcript of Huang's June 2026 keynote. It confirms the $80–100B per GW figure. 190 × 80–100 gives $15.2–19T, not $9.5–15T. Secondary source, but its quote matches the stated input.

reviews.rationale: At Zitron's own inputs, 190GW times $80–100B per GW is $15.2–19T. His stated range of $9.5–15T matches roughly $50–79B per GW instead. Both endpoints are materially off, so the claimed result of the calculation is contradicted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, addressed to tech executives.

semantics.note: A sweeping, polemical causal claim: AI mandates have radicalized employees at major tech firms. The normalised version keeps both the scope and the causal link.

contract.note: Reading 'radicalized' as materially more hostility toward leadership, without implying extremism, is fair and ordinary. Requiring a broad pattern fits the 'any major tech company' framing. The threshold is still a matter of interpretation.

evidence.note: Open letter from Amazon employees tying forced AI use to opposition against leadership. It covers only one firm, its signers chose to sign, and it mixes in other grievances. Labelled a company disclosure, but it actually comes from an employee group.
Fortune report confirming the letter existed. Over 1,000 signers out of about 1.53M staff. Says nothing on how widespread this is or what caused it.
WRITER survey commentary on tension around AI adoption. It does not isolate tech workers, mandates, or attitudes toward leadership.
Gallup Q1 2026 survey, published August 2026, before the cutoff. Culture effects of AI were mixed (25% said worse, 24% better). Broad population, not people facing mandates.

reviews.rationale: Only one firm's self-selected letter partly supports the causal link. The surveys do not isolate mandated tech workers or measure attitudes before and after. Gallup's mixed results weigh against a sweeping effect but do not contradict it. The packet does not settle the broad causal claim.
